EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

====================================================================  
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID), supplemented by a triple-difference robustness check.  

Rationale  
• We observe the same restaurants immediately before and 7–8 months after the policy.  
• A clearly “untreated” geographic control group (eastern Pennsylvania) is available, exposed to the same macro conditions but not to the higher wage floor.  
• The shock is discrete, externally imposed, and its timing is known (April 1 1992).  
• The short pre/post window—and the fact that wages in the fast-food sector cluster at or near the legal minimum—make contamination by other policies unlikely.  
Given these features, DID is the canonical, most transparent approach.  

====================================================================  
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if the restaurant is located in New Jersey AND the observation is in the post-policy wave; 0 otherwise.  

Control groups  
Primary: Eastern-PA stores surveyed in the same two waves.  
Secondary (for robustness / triple diff):  
 • NJ stores that already paid ≥ $5.05 in February–March (essentially “high-wage” NJ).  

Timing  
Pre = Wave 1 (Feb–Mar 1992).  
Post = Wave 2 (Nov–Dec 1992).  
Policy date: April 1 1992.  

No running variable or cutoff is needed because we are not exploiting cross-sectional forcing around a threshold (RDD).  

====================================================================  
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the NJ increase, outcomes in NJ and eastern-PA stores would have evolved similarly from spring to winter 1992.  
 • Plausibility: Restaurants are in the same macro region, belong to identical chains, face similar seasonality. Pre-policy CPS teen-employment trends (NJ vs. PA) can be plotted to support this.  

A2. No spillovers/contamination: The NJ hike did not induce Pennsylvania stores to raise pay or change staffing in response to cross-border labor flows or competitive pressure.  
 • Plausibility: The sample is limited to eastern-PA counties, some contiguous to NJ, so labor-market spillovers are possible but should be modest because commuting costs are high for low-wage teenagers. We can test wage changes in PA stores directly.  

A3. Stable composition: Store closure, opening, or survey attrition must not be systematically related to treatment.  
 • Plausibility: 100 % follow-up on closures and a very short window mitigate survivorship bias.  

A4. No differential anticipation: Because the hike was enacted in 1990 and could have been repealed only three days before 4/1/92, advance adjustments are limited and symmetrically affect both groups.  

A5. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): The treatment status of one store does not change the potential outcomes of another except through general-equilibrium wage spillovers already discussed in A2.  

====================================================================  
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATIONS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Macroeconomic divergence / NJ-specific recession shock.  
 Fix:  
 • Include county-by-month or state-by-month fixed effects using high-frequency data (CPS teen employment) in triple-difference.  
 • Test pre-treatment equivalence using 1988–91 CPS trends.  

2. Cross-border spillovers into PA (wage or employment reactions).  
 Fix:  
 • Estimate DID on wages in PA. If PA wages remain at $4.25, contamination is minimal.  
 • Drop PA counties bordering NJ as a robustness check.  

3. Selection through store closures/openings.  
 Fix:  
 • Use the verified closure information: treat closed stores as zero employment in Wave 2 (intent-to-treat).  
 • Implement inverse-probability weighting if any attrition remains.  

====================================================================  
5. R CODE OUTLINE  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)   # fast manipulation
library(fixest)       # high-quality DID / FE regressions
library(modelsummary) # nice tables

# 1. Load data (assumed CSVs)
stores   <- fread("fastfood_store_survey.csv")      # main two-wave survey
cpsteen  <- fread("CPS_teen_state_monthly.csv")     # for robustness

# 2. Variable construction
stores[, post  := (wave == 2)]                       # 1 = Nov–Dec 92
stores[, nj    := (state == "NJ")]
stores[, treat := nj * post]                         # interaction term

# Outcomes
yvars <- c("fte_employment", "starting_wage",
           "meal_price", "fringe_meal", "recruit_bonus")

# 3. Main DID specification
#   y_ist = α + β Treat_st + δ_i + γ_t + ε_ist
did_results <- lapply(yvars, function(v) {
  feols(as.formula(paste0(v, " ~ treat | store_id + post")), data = stores)
})

modelsummary(did_results, stars = TRUE,
             title = "Difference-in-Differences Estimates of NJ Minimum-Wage Rise")

# 4. Robustness check 1: triple difference
stores[, high_wage_pre := (starting_wage_pre >= 5.05)]
stores[, ddiff := treat * !high_wage_pre] # effect only for low-wage NJ stores
triple <- feols(fte_employment ~ ddiff | store_id + post + nj, data = stores)

# 5. Robustness check 2: drop PA border counties
stores_noborder <- stores[border_pa == 0]
did_noborder <- feols(fte_employment ~ treat | store_id + post, data = stores_noborder)
```

====================================================================  
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory under perfectly competitive labor markets suggests a 10 % wage increase should cut labor demand roughly one-for-one with elasticity –0.1 to –0.3 ⇒ employment fall of 1–3 %.  
However, monopsony / search models and prior empirical work predict near-zero or even positive employment changes.  
Prior:  
• Wages: +18–20 % at the bottom tail.  
• Employment (FTE): 0 % to –2 % (statistically indistinguishable from zero).  
• Prices: +2–4 %.  
• Fringe benefits: small negative adjustments (e.g., fewer free meals).  

====================================================================  
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
C1 (Parallel trends credible from pre-treatment evidence)…… 1  
C2 (No simultaneous confounders differing by group/time)…… 1  
C3 (No anticipatory behavior or lagged treatment response)…… 0.5  
C4 (No spillovers between treated and controls)……………… 0.5  
C5 (Stable sample / no differential attrition)………………… 1  

Total = 4/5 ⇒ overall internal validity judged “high but not perfect.”
